young.html: Max Planck was a German physicist, a careful, patient man who also played the piano beautifully. Near the end of his long life he wrote a short story of how he made the discovery that started quantum physics.

The puzzle he worked on was about glowing things. Heat a poker in a fire: first it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white. Stars glow too, and their colors tell how hot they are. In 1900 Planck found the exact rule for how much of each color a hot object gives off.

To make his rule work, he had to make a strange guess: that energy doesn’t flow out smoothly, like water from a tap, but in tiny packets, like coins. He called each packet a quantum. Blue light comes in bigger packets than red light. Planck himself was not sure at first that the packets were real. They were.

young.cap: Slide the temperature. Hotter bodies glow brighter and their peak color moves from red toward blue.

young.html: Color thermometer. With a grown-up, look at different lights: a candle flame, an old-style yellowish bulb, a bright white LED, a blue gas flame on a stove (from a safe distance). Line them up from “coolest” color to “hottest.” Astronomers do the same with stars: red stars are cooler, blue-white stars are hotter.

full.html: Max Planck (1858–1947) was born in Kiel and became professor of theoretical physics in Berlin in 1889. His first love in physics was the law of the conservation of energy, and his early work was on thermodynamics, the science of heat. In 1900 he found the law of blackbody radiation and, to explain it, introduced the quantum of action, $h$. He received the Nobel Prize in 1918 and was for decades the most respected figure in German science.

Scientific Autobiography and Other Papers appeared in English in 1949 (the autobiography itself was published in German in 1948), translated by Frank Gaynor. It gathers his short memoir of his scientific life with several lectures on what science can and can’t know, among them “Phantom Problems in Science” and “The Meaning and Limits of Exact Science.”
These essays were first published in English in 1949, so they are still under copyright, and this rung quotes none of them. Everything here is our own summary.

full.text: The problem: the color of heat

full.html: A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs all light falling on it; heated, it glows with a spectrum that depends only on its temperature. Gustav Kirchhoff had shown in 1859 that this spectrum is a universal law of nature, which made it, for Planck, a search for something absolute. By the late 1890s, careful measurements in Berlin by Otto Lummer, Ernst Pringsheim, Heinrich Rubens and Ferdinand Kurlbaum showed that the best formula of the day (Wien’s) failed at long wavelengths. Another formula, from classical physics (later called the Rayleigh–Jeans law), worked at long wavelengths but predicted infinite brightness at short ones, an impossibility later called the ultraviolet catastrophe.

full.name: gb-blackbody
full.cap: Planck’s law (solid) and the older classical formula (dashed). They agree far to the right; at short wavelengths the old formula shoots upward without limit.

full.html: In October 1900 Planck found a formula that fit all the measurements: Rubens checked it against his data the next day. Then came weeks of what Planck describes as the hardest work of his life, to find out why it was true. He could derive it only by assuming that the energy of the vibrating sources of light comes in whole-number multiples of a small unit, $E = hf$, where $f$ is the frequency. He presented this on 14 December 1900, the date often called the birthday of quantum theory. For years he hoped the quanta could be fitted back into classical physics. It was Einstein (1905), and later Bohr, who took them to be real.

Planck’s two formulas. Each quantum of light carries energy $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s. And the peak of a blackbody’s glow (Wien’s displacement law) is at $\lambda_{\text{peak}} \approx 2.898 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m·K} \div T$.

full.title: The Sun’s color
full.q: The Sun’s surface is about 5,800 K. At what wavelength does its light peak?
steps: $= 5.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m $= 500$ nm: blue-green, in the middle of visible light.

full.title: One quantum of green light
full.q: How much energy is in one quantum (photon) of green light with wavelength 500 nm?
full.a: About $4 \times 10^{-19}$ joules, which is why we never notice single quanta.

full.html: The autobiography also tells of Planck’s early disappointments. As a young man he could not get the leading physicists of the day to take his ideas on entropy seriously; they hardly read his work. From this he drew a sober lesson that is now called Planck’s principle: a new scientific truth usually wins not because its opponents are persuaded, but because they eventually pass away and a new generation grows up familiar with it. Historians and sociologists of science still debate how often that is so.

In the other papers Planck argues that some famous puzzles are “phantom problems,” questions that look deep only because they are badly posed, and that exact science reaches real knowledge of an outside world even though it can never be complete. He writes about religion and science as compatible; readers will judge that view for themselves.
Thinking Planck set out to start a revolution. He was a cautious, conservative physicist who reached the quantum reluctantly, because the measurements left no other way.

full.text: His life and how it was judged

full.html: Planck’s quantum is the foundation of modern physics, chemistry and electronics; the constant $h$ is now used to define the kilogram (since 2019). His personal life held great sorrows: his first wife and four of his five children died before him: his son Karl was killed in the First World War, his twin daughters died in childbirth, and his son Erwin was executed by the Nazi regime in 1945 for his ties to the plot against Hitler. Planck stayed in Germany through the Nazi years, trying to protect science and colleagues; historians have discussed how much such quiet efforts could do. After the war the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, which he had led, was renamed the Max Planck Society.

items: Newton’s Optics and Huygens’s Treatise on Light, earlier on this ladder, argued over particles and waves. Planck’s quanta reopened the question.
Faraday and Maxwell made light an electromagnetic wave; Planck found that its energy still comes in packets.
Bohr used Planck’s $E = hf$ to explain the colors of hydrogen; Heisenberg, the next rung, built the new mechanics on $h$.
Kuhn’s later account of scientific revolutions made much of Planck’s principle about generations.
Why might a person who discovers something new be the slowest to accept it?
Is it true that new ideas win only when the old guard passes away? What else can change minds?
Planck searched for laws that hold everywhere and for everyone. Is that what science is for?

questions: What colors does a fire or a stove burner glow? What do the colors tell you?
Planck made a guess he didn’t believe at first. Why might a scientist publish a guess like that?
Planck said new ideas often win only when a new generation grows up with them. Do you think that is true at home or at school?
Planck lost several of his children and lived through two world wars, yet kept working. What helps people keep going?
Energy comes in tiny packets we never notice. What other things look smooth but are made of tiny pieces?
